query: For high-value components operating in aggressive environments, what intervention could improve surface physical and mechanical characteristics? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence that would support it, and an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing electrospark deposition (ESD) using a multicomponent electrode with a bonding mass of 25–35% Co-Ni-Cr-B-Si alloy and superhard particles (WC, B4C, TiB2) will produce a composite coating that markedly improves surface microhardness, adhesion, and wear resistance on high-value carbon steel components operating in aggressive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: High-value carbon steel components (e.g., C45) with untreated surfaces exhibiting standard wear, adhesion, and microhardness characteristics.
generation.intervention: Application of an optimized ESD coating using multicomponent electrodes containing 25–35% bonding mass and reinforcing superhard particles (WC, B4C, TiB2) with controlled pulse energy.
generation.conditions: Operating under aggressive environments (high wear and friction conditions at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures) where rapid surface degradation is normally observed.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, uniform composite coating featuring a crystalline-amorphous matrix interspersed with intermetallic, carbide, boride, and nitride phases that provide mechanical reinforcement and improved adhesion.
generation.mechanism: The ESD process generates a composite structure where the metallic bonding phase ensures excellent substrate adhesion, while the dispersed superhard reinforcements enhance microhardness and reduce abrasion. The synergy between these phases minimizes wear by distributing loads and resisting deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The resulting coating will exhibit an increase in microhardness (approaching the upper range of 15.0 GPa compared to untreated values around 8.5 GPa), improved adhesion, and wear rates up to 5 times lower than the uncoated substrate under similar conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated carbon steel surfaces that show lower microhardness, poorer adhesion, and higher wear rates in aggressive environments.
generation.boundary: The improvements are anticipated only for components amenable to ESD processing and within the optimal coating thickness (8–65 µm) and roughness (Ra 1.5–7 µm) ranges; performance may vary if applied to materials or geometries outside these parameters.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements may depend on slight variations in electrode composition, pulse energy settings, and substrate properties; scaling the process to components outside small-to-medium sizes introduces additional variables.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of high-value carbon steel test components, applying the optimized ESD coating to half using the specified electrode composition and parameters, while leaving the other half untreated. Expose both sets to identical accelerated wear testing regimes under simulated aggressive environmental conditions, including controlled friction, load, and temperature cycles.
measurements: Microhardness (GPa) across the coated and uncoated surfaces
Wear rate or mass loss over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 20% increase in microhardness and a corresponding reduction in wear rate by a fraction approaching the anticipated 5-fold decrease) compared to the untreated baseline under identical test conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractThis work demonstrates the possibility of creating effective composite coatings with a complex structure and phase composition on carbon steel C45 via electrospark deposition (ESD) with multicomponent electrodes with a bonding mass composition of Co-Ni-Cr-B-Si semi-self-fluxing alloys and superhard compounds WC, B4C and TiB2. The variation in the roughness, thickness, composition, structure, microhardness and wear at the friction of the coatings as a function of the ratios between the bonding mass and the high-hardness components in the composition of the electrode and of the pulse energy for ESD has been studied. It has been established that with a content of the bonding mass in the electrode of 25–35%, coatings with improved adhesion and simultaneously higher hardness and toughness are obtained. Suitable electrode compositions and optimal pulse energy have been defined, which provide dense and uniform coatings with an increased amount of crystalline-amorphous structures, as well as intermetallic and wear-resistant phases, with thickness, roughness and microhardness that can be changed by the ESD modes in the ranges of δ = 8–65 µm, Ra = 1.5–7 µm, and HV 8.5–15.

In addition, they cannot provide coating thicknesses above 30 µm, good adhesion and application on complex surfaces. Laser coating tools and equipment are complex and expensive, and it is difficult to achieve a coating on a product with complex geometry. The ion–plasma nitriding process takes 3–6 h, and the formation of cathodic arcs damages the surface during processing. Flame spraying requires pre-texturing and heating and post-treatment of the coated surfaces. Some of the methods are too expensive and can only be used for applications where the high cost is justified.
